standard.title: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts
standard.description: plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising and expanding ideas, and selecting text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features for purposes and audiences in ways that may be imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive and/or analytical
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can plan, create, edit and publish texts for a range of purposes and audiences, making deliberate text structure and language feature choices (AC9E7LY06). They have not yet focused on expanding and organising ideas through the full planning-to-publishing cycle with academic accuracy goals, or on the deliberate use of vocabulary for positioning and persuasion.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts, organising and expanding ideas with deliberate structural, language and visual feature choices suited to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Planning and organising ideas
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can plan a written or multimodal text by organising and expanding ideas — using conceptual maps, journals or equivalent tools — and selecting appropriate text structures for the text's purpose and audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Produce a planning document (conceptual map, outline or journal) for a written text that organises and expands at least three ideas and identifies the text structure to be used.
nodes.typical_width: Plan written and multimodal texts using conceptual maps or journals to organise and expand ideas; select appropriate text structures and justify how these selections serve the text's purpose and audience; plan for the integration of language features, literary devices and visual features.
wider: Compare different planning approaches (linear outline vs conceptual map vs journal drafting) and evaluate which approach produces better-organised ideas for a specific text type
Plan a multimodal text that requires explicit decisions about how written text, images and visual layout will work together to serve the purpose and audience
Investigate how published authors describe their planning process and compare with own practice — examining whether planning strategies vary by text type or purpose

response_modes.reason: Planning a text with deliberate structural and language feature choices requires students to separate planning decisions from execution — an unfamiliar metacognitive move. Without explicit scaffolding of what a planning document should contain (ideas, structure, feature selections), students either skip planning or treat it as an outline with no selection rationale.

success_criteria: Produces a planning document that organises ideas and identifies a text structure suited to the purpose.
Can explain why the chosen structure is appropriate for the text's purpose and intended audience.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to create texts with deliberate structural and language feature selections — which presupposes a plan that has already organised ideas and identified structural choices. Thin planning means students create reactively rather than deliberately, making the 'deliberate selection' evidence invisible.

nodes.label: Creating with deliberate language and feature selection
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create written or multimodal texts that make deliberate selections from text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features to serve their purposes and audiences.
nodes.minimum_width: Create a text for a specified purpose and audience that demonstrates at least two deliberate selection choices (e.g. a specific text structure, a vocabulary choice to position the reader, or a literary device for effect) and can explain each choice.
nodes.typical_width: Create written and multimodal texts for a range of purposes (imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive, analytical) and audiences, making deliberate and explainable selections from text structures, language features, literary devices and visual features; select vocabulary to position and persuade the reader where appropriate.
wider: Create a text that deliberately exploits the conventions of a specific genre for persuasive or satirical effect — using the reader's genre expectations as a rhetorical tool
Create a multimodal text in which visual features and written text work interdependently, and reflect on how each modality contributes differently to the overall purpose

Create a text for an unfamiliar audience (e.g. a First Nations community audience, an academic audience, an international audience) and reflect on what structural and language choices the unfamiliar audience requires

response_modes.reason: Creating across the range of text purposes (imaginative, informative, persuasive, analytical) requires a repertoire of structural and language strategies associated with each purpose. Students who have only created in one mode cannot transfer confidently to others. Multiple creation tasks across purposes build this repertoire.

success_criteria: Creates a text for a named purpose and audience.
Can identify and explain at least two deliberate structural or language choices made in the text and how they serve the purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 is editing for accuracy and meaning. Effective editing requires a text that was created with deliberate choices — something to evaluate and refine. Students who created without repertoire at Node 2 have only mechanical errors to correct at Node 3, not purposeful revision decisions to make. The editing task collapses to proofreading.

nodes.label: Editing for accuracy and meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can edit own texts for grammatical accuracy, spelling and punctuation, and for clarity and precision of meaning — using experimentation with sentence structure, literary devices and vocabulary to clarify ideas.
nodes.minimum_width: Edit a piece of own writing for at least one grammatical feature (sentence structure, punctuation or spelling) and for at least one meaning clarity revision, and explain the revisions made.
nodes.typical_width: Edit written texts for accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation, and for meaning — experimenting with sentence structure order, literary devices and vocabulary to clarify ideas for academic or creative purposes; reflect on how editing decisions change the text.
wider: Conduct a systematic editing cycle — first for accuracy, then for meaning, then for effect — and document the revision history with annotations explaining each change
Edit a peer's writing for meaning clarity and accuracy, providing written justifications for suggested revisions
Examine published author revisions (where available) and compare editorial decisions with own editing practice

response_modes.reason: Editing fluency requires repeated practice — the habit of reading one's own writing critically for accuracy and meaning does not develop from a single editing task. Multiple edit cycles across varied texts, with explicit attention to different editing foci, build the automaticity that makes editing reliable rather than superficial.

success_criteria: Produces a revised version of own text with identifiable improvements to at least one grammatical feature and at least one meaning clarity issue.
Can explain the rationale for at least two specific editing decisions.
